questions.q: Why does a deep network with only linear layers have no more expressive power than one linear layer?
options: A composition of linear maps is itself a linear map
questions.why: $W_2(W_1x) = (W_2W_1)x$. Nonlinear activations between layers are what allow deep networks to represent complex functions.

questions.q: Which activation can cause "dead" units that never recover?
options: ReLU, when a unit's input is negative for every example
questions.why: ReLU's gradient is zero for negative inputs, so a unit pushed into that region gets no updates. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope.

questions.q: Xavier/Glorot initialisation scales weights by $\sqrt{2/(\text{fan\_in} + \text{fan\_out})}$. Which activation was it designed for?
questions.why: It keeps activation and gradient variances roughly constant for activations that are linear near zero. He initialisation adjusts for ReLU.

questions.q: In the backward pass of softmax with cross-entropy, the gradient at the logits is...
questions.why: The softmax Jacobian and the log combine into prediction minus target, which is why the two are usually fused.

questions.q: A mini-batch training loop should save a checkpoint based on which metric?
questions.why: Training loss keeps falling as the model overfits. The best validation checkpoint is the one to keep.

questions.q: Channel dropout (`Dropout2d`) drops what?
questions.why: Neighbouring pixels in a feature map are strongly correlated, so dropping single pixels barely regularises; dropping whole channels does.

questions.q: BatchNorm at inference uses which statistics?
options: Zero mean and unit variance always
questions.why: Inference batches may be size 1 or unrepresentative, so the layer uses stored estimates. Forgetting `eval()` is a common bug.

questions.q: Autograd with broadcasting: `y = x + b` where `x` is `(N, D)` and `b` is `(D,)`. What is the gradient for `b`?
options: The upstream gradient itself, shape `(N, D)`
The mean over the batch axis
The upstream gradient summed over the batch axis
questions.why: A broadcast input was used $N$ times, so its gradient sums the contributions back to its own shape.

questions.q: A 3×3 convolution with stride 1 and padding 1 on a 32×32 input gives what output size?
questions.why: $\lfloor(32 + 2\cdot1 - 3)/1\rfloor + 1 = 32$. "Same" padding for odd kernels is $(k - 1)/2$.

questions.q: Two stacked 3×3 convolutions have the same receptive field as one...
options: 5×5 convolution, with fewer parameters and an extra nonlinearity
questions.why: Each adds 2 to the receptive field. Two 3×3 layers use $18C^2$ weights against $25C^2$, the reasoning behind VGG.

questions.q: What does a dilation of 2 do to a 3×3 kernel's receptive field?
options: Expands it to 5×5 without adding parameters
questions.why: Dilation spaces the taps apart, letting the network see wider context cheaply, as in segmentation models.

questions.q: Depthwise separable convolution reduces cost by roughly what factor for kernel size $k$ and $C_{out}$ output channels?
options: About $1/C_{out} + 1/k^2$ of a standard convolution's cost
questions.why: A per-channel $k\times k$ filter plus a 1×1 pointwise mix costs a small fraction of a full $k\times k\times C_{in}\times C_{out}$ convolution, the basis of MobileNet.

questions.q: Transposed convolution with stride 2 is commonly used for what?
options: Learned upsampling, roughly doubling the spatial size
questions.why: It scatters each input pixel into a larger output. Uneven overlaps can produce checkerboard artefacts; resize-then-convolve avoids them.

questions.q: Why does a ResNet block use a projection shortcut sometimes?
options: When the block changes the number of channels or the spatial size, so the shapes can be added
questions.why: Identity shortcuts need matching shapes; a strided 1×1 convolution fixes the mismatch.

questions.q: The Inception module uses 1×1 convolutions before 3×3 and 5×5 branches. Why?
options: To reduce channels and so the cost of the larger convolutions
questions.why: Bottlenecking the channel count makes running several kernel sizes in parallel affordable.

questions.q: Max pooling with a 2×2 window and stride 2 passes gradients to which inputs?
options: Only the maximum element of each window
questions.why: The other elements didn't affect the output, so their gradient is zero. Average pooling would split the gradient evenly.

questions.q: Why do vanilla RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies?
options: Gradients through many time steps vanish or explode as they are repeatedly multiplied by the recurrent Jacobian
questions.why: Repeated multiplication by matrices with norms below or above 1 shrinks or blows up the signal exponentially in the number of steps.

questions.q: Which part of an LSTM lets gradients flow across many steps?
options: The cell state, updated additively and scaled by the forget gate
The tanh on the hidden state
questions.why: When the forget gate is near 1, the cell state passes through almost unchanged, giving a near-identity gradient path.

questions.q: A GRU differs from an LSTM how?
options: It merges the cell and hidden state and uses two gates instead of three
questions.why: GRUs are a little cheaper and often perform similarly.

questions.q: Teacher forcing during seq2seq training means what?
options: Training with a larger learning rate
Forcing the encoder to copy the input
Feeding the ground-truth previous token to the decoder rather than its own prediction
questions.why: It speeds up training but creates exposure bias: at inference the decoder sees its own mistakes, which it never saw in training.

questions.q: Initialising the LSTM forget-gate bias to 1 or more helps because...
options: The cell starts by remembering, so gradients flow across time early in training
It speeds up the forward pass
questions.why: With a zero bias the forget gate starts near 0.5, halving the memory every step.

questions.q: Gradient clipping is standard for RNN training because...
options: Exploding gradients across time steps can produce huge updates
It is required for teacher forcing
questions.why: Clipping caps the update size; it doesn't fix vanishing gradients, which gated architectures address.

questions.q: An Elman RNN over padded sequences should take the final hidden state from where?
options: Each sequence's last real time step, not the padded end
The average over all steps including padding
The last time step of the padded batch for all sequences
questions.why: Steps after the real end process padding and change the state. Gather the state at `length - 1` or mask the updates.

questions.q: How many parameters does an LSTM layer with input size $d$ and hidden size $h$ have (with biases)?
questions.why: Four gates, each with input weights, recurrent weights and a bias. (PyTorch keeps two bias vectors per gate, giving $4(dh + h^2 + 2h)$.)

questions.q: Self-attention's cost in sequence length $n$ and width $d$ is...
questions.why: Every token scores every other token. The projections cost $O(nd^2)$, which dominates for short sequences.

questions.q: Pre-LN versus post-LN transformer blocks: which is easier to train deep without warmup?
options: Neither can be trained without warmup
Pre-LN, because the residual path is never normalised and gradients reach early layers directly
questions.why: Post-LN normalises after the residual add, which makes gradients near the output large at initialisation. Most modern LLMs use pre-norm.

questions.q: Why do transformers need positional information?
options: Attention is permutation-invariant; without positions, word order is lost
questions.why: Shuffling the input tokens would just shuffle the outputs. Learned, sinusoidal or rotary encodings break that symmetry.

questions.q: RoPE makes the query-key score depend on positions how?
options: Through the absolute position of the query only
questions.why: Rotating $q$ by $m\theta$ and $k$ by $n\theta$ leaves the dot product depending on $(m - n)\theta$, giving relative-position attention.

questions.q: In a decoder block with cross-attention, where do the keys and values come from?
questions.why: Queries come from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder, letting each output position look at the source sequence.

questions.q: The backward pass of LayerNorm is not elementwise because...
options: Each output depends on every input in its row through the mean and variance
questions.why: The gradient subtracts the row mean of the upstream gradient and its projection on the normalised values.

questions.q: ViT prepends a learnable class token. What is it used for?
options: Its final representation feeds the classification head
It marks the end of the image
questions.why: Through attention the token aggregates information from all patches. Global average pooling of patch tokens is a common alternative.

questions.q: Grouped-query attention reduces what at inference?
options: The KV cache size, by sharing key-value heads across query heads
questions.why: Fewer KV heads means less memory traffic per decode step, which is often the bottleneck.

questions.q: Tied weights in an autoencoder mean what?
options: Encoder and decoder share biases only
The decoder uses the transpose of the encoder's weight matrix
questions.why: Tying halves the parameters and acts as a regulariser.

questions.q: The VAE's ELBO consists of which two terms?
options: Expected reconstruction log-likelihood minus the KL divergence from the encoder distribution to the prior
questions.why: Maximising it trains the encoder and decoder together. The KL term keeps the latent space close to the prior so you can sample from it.

questions.q: Why is the reparameterisation trick needed in a VAE?
options: To make the KL term zero
It writes $z = \mu + \sigma\epsilon$ so gradients can flow through the sampling step to $\mu$ and $\sigma$
questions.why: Sampling $z$ directly from $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ isn't differentiable in $\mu$ and $\sigma$; moving the randomness into $\epsilon$ fixes that.

questions.q: In a GAN, the generator's non-saturating loss is $-\log D(G(z))$. Why prefer it to $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$?
options: It is the original minimax objective
It gives strong gradients early on, when the discriminator easily rejects fakes
questions.why: When $D(G(z)) \approx 0$, $\log(1 - D)$ is flat, so the generator learns little. The alternative has the same fixed point.

questions.q: Mode collapse in a GAN means what?
options: The generator produces only a few kinds of output, ignoring much of the data distribution
questions.why: The generator can fool the discriminator with a narrow set of samples. Techniques like minibatch discrimination or other objectives mitigate it.

questions.q: A VAE's samples are often blurrier than a GAN's. Why?
options: A Gaussian reconstruction loss averages over plausible outputs
The KL term adds noise to samples
questions.why: Pixel-wise likelihood rewards predicting the mean of possible images, which is blurry. Adversarial losses reward realism instead.

questions.q: What does a VAE's KL term equal for a diagonal Gaussian encoder and a standard normal prior?
questions.why: The closed form is cheap and differentiable, so no sampling is needed for this term.

questions.q: Which component of a GAN gets gradients from the real data directly?
questions.why: The generator sees real data only through the discriminator's judgement.

questions.q: Non-maximum suppression removes boxes that...
options: Have low IoU with all boxes
Overlap a higher-scoring box of the same class by more than an IoU threshold
questions.why: Greedy NMS keeps the best box and suppresses its near-duplicates. Class-aware NMS only compares boxes of the same class.

questions.q: A squeeze-and-excitation block gates channels using what?
options: A small MLP on globally pooled channel statistics, ending in a sigmoid
questions.why: It learns per-channel weights from global context at little cost, adding a few percent of parameters.

questions.q: A U-Net decoder step concatenates upsampled features with what?
options: The encoder features at the same resolution (skip connection)
questions.why: Skip connections bring back fine spatial detail lost during downsampling. With valid convolutions the encoder features must be cropped to match.

questions.q: Why does NMS use an IoU threshold rather than any overlap?
options: Different objects can overlap slightly; only near-duplicates should be removed
questions.why: Typical thresholds are 0.5 to 0.7. Crowded scenes need higher thresholds or soft-NMS.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of skip connections in very deep networks?
options: To provide direct paths for gradients and let blocks learn residuals
questions.why: With an identity path, a block can default to doing nothing, and gradients reach early layers without passing through every transformation.

questions.q: Attention-style gating (SE, CBAM) helps CNNs by...
options: Reweighting features based on global context
Increasing the receptive field to infinity
questions.why: Recalibrating channels or spatial positions lets the network emphasise informative features.

questions.q: Knowledge distillation trains a small model on what?
options: The large model's softened output distribution, often mixed with the true labels
questions.why: Soft targets carry information about which wrong classes are similar, which hard labels lack. A temperature softens the teacher's softmax.

questions.q: Mixed-precision training keeps a float32 copy of the weights. Why?
options: Float16 can't be used for matmuls
Small updates added to float16 weights would be rounded away
questions.why: The master copy accumulates tiny updates accurately while the forward and backward passes run in half precision.
